subject: operating-systems
name: Operating Systems
exam: TU assessment: 60% final examination set by the university, 40% internal (assignments, lab work, attendance).

units.title: Introduction to Operating Systems
topics: History and generations of operating systems
Key hardware ideas an OS relies on
Seeing the ideas: three machines, two roles, one utilisation curve

sections.title: History and generations of operating systems
Key hardware ideas an OS relies on
Seeing the ideas: three machines, two roles, one utilisation curve

summary: An OS is the privileged layer that manages hardware and offers abstractions (files, processes, address spaces) to applications.
It acts both as an extended machine and as a resource manager.
OS history is a history of keeping the CPU busy: batch, multiprogramming, time-sharing, personal computers, distributed and mobile systems.
Batch, time-sharing, real-time, distributed, network, embedded and mobile OS types differ in their main goal: throughput, response time, deadlines, transparency, or power and footprint.
Interrupts, a timer, protection registers and the user/kernel mode bit are the hardware that makes an OS possible.

units.title: Operating System Structure
topics: Seeing the ideas: shells, kernels and hypervisors

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: shells, kernels and hypervisors

summary: System calls are the controlled entry into the kernel; most programs use APIs built on them.
Monolithic kernels trade safety for speed; layered designs make verification easy; microkernels move services to user space for reliability; exokernels expose raw hardware.
The client-server model and VMs extend the same idea of separating services from each other.
The shell is only a program; the kernel is what makes it possible.

units.title: Process Management
topics: Seeing the ideas: states, races, semaphores and schedules

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: states, races, semaphores and schedules

summary: A process is a program in execution described by a PCB; it moves among new, ready, running, waiting and terminated; fork, exec, wait and exit manage it.
Threads share the address space but have their own stacks and registers; one-to-one is the dominant model.

Unsynchronised access to shared data creates race conditions; the critical-section solution needs mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting. Peterson and TSL use busy waiting; semaphores, monitors and message passing block instead.

The classical problems (bounded buffer, dining philosophers, readers-writers, sleeping barber) are templates for real synchronization bugs. Two-phase locking and timestamps give serializable transaction schedules.
Scheduling algorithms trade throughput, turnaround, waiting and response time: SJF/SRTF minimise waiting, RR gives fairness, MLFQ adapts, RMS/EDF handle deadlines.

units.title: Deadlocks
topics: The ostrich algorithm and methods of handling deadlocks
Seeing the ideas: gridlock, graphs and the Banker

sections.title: The ostrich algorithm and methods of handling deadlocks
Seeing the ideas: gridlock, graphs and the Banker

summary: Deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait; breaking any one prevents it.
RAGs show deadlocks as cycles (certain with single instances).
Strategies: ostrich, prevention (ordering resources is most practical), avoidance (Banker's), detection with recovery.
The Banker's algorithm keeps the system in safe states using maximum claims. Detection uses the same logic with current requests.
Recovery means killing processes or preempting resources, while watching out for starvation.

units.title: Memory Management
topics: Seeing the ideas: memory, swap space and the page table

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: memory, swap space and the page table

summary: The MMU maps logical to physical addresses; base and limit registers give relocation and protection.
Contiguous allocation suffers fragmentation; fit strategies, coalescing and compaction mitigate it.
Paging removes external fragmentation; page tables are made practical by multilevel, hashed and inverted structures and the TLB.
Demand paging loads pages on first use; page faults are costly, so the replacement policy matters. OPT is a lower bound, LRU approximates it, FIFO is simple but anomalous.
Thrashing results when working sets do not fit; segmentation offers a programmer's view and combines with paging.

units.title: Input/Output Device Management
topics: Seeing the ideas: interrupt controllers, disks and head movement

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: interrupt controllers, disks and head movement

summary: Devices are block or character; each has a controller reached through ports or memory-mapped registers.
DMA lets the controller move whole blocks and interrupt the CPU once.
I/O software aims for device independence, uniform naming, buffering and error handling; it is layered (handler, driver, device-independent, user).
Disk time is dominated by seek and rotation, so the arm is scheduled: SSTF is greedy, SCAN and C-SCAN sweep, LOOK variants save needless travel.

units.title: File System Interface Management
topics: File-system layout and allocation (what the interface hides)
Seeing the ideas: tapes, card indexes and directory trees

sections.title: File-system layout and allocation (what the interface hides)
Seeing the ideas: tapes, card indexes and directory trees

summary: A file is a named, persistent collection of bytes with attributes; a file descriptor is the handle returned by open.
Directories are organised as trees (or graphs with links); paths are absolute or relative.
Access is sequential or direct. Inodes, linked and contiguous allocation are the implementations behind the interface.
Protection uses permission bits, ACLs and capabilities, ideally with least privilege.

units.title: Security Management
topics: Seeing the ideas: tokens, keys, fingerprints and attacks

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: tokens, keys, fingerprints and attacks

summary: Security aims at confidentiality, integrity and availability and must be applied at physical, human, OS and network levels.
Passwords are weak against guessing and brute force; they must be stored salted and hashed; longer is far better than "complex".
OTPs (HOTP/TOTP), tokens and biometrics add factors; authorization applies least privilege after login.
Program threats (Trojan, trap door, buffer overflow) abuse trust in code; system threats (viruses, worms, DoS) abuse trust in the network and the host.

units.title: Distributed Operating Systems
topics: Processes and threads in distributed systems
Seeing the ideas: nodes, clocks and message diagrams

sections.title: Processes and threads in distributed systems
Seeing the ideas: nodes, clocks and message diagrams

summary: A distributed system is independent computers that look like one; it gives economy, speed, reliability and growth at the price of complexity, networking and security problems.
Hardware divides into multiprocessors and multicomputers; software into network OS, distributed OS and middleware.
Message passing and RPC are the basic communication tools; RPC hides messaging but not failures or latency.
Clocks drift, so Cristian's and Berkeley's algorithms and NTP synchronise physical clocks, while Lamport clocks give a consistent order of events.

units.title: Case Study: DOS, Windows, UNIX and Linux
topics: Seeing the ideas: four systems side by side

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: four systems side by side

summary: MS-DOS shows what a minimal OS looks like and why protection and multitasking were needed.
Windows NT adds a layered hybrid design, preemptive priority scheduling, NTFS and a security model with ACLs.
UNIX contributed portability, a unified file abstraction and small cooperating tools.
Linux combines the UNIX design with open-source development, loadable modules and a fair scheduler.
